answers.label: Q.1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: A successful leader leads by example, communicates well with teammates, takes the right decisions, motivates everyone, stays calm in a crisis and out-thinks rivals.
answers.solution:
According to the author, a successful leader leads by example and communicates well with his teammates. He takes the right decisions, motivates everyone to give their best, remains calm in times of crisis and out-thinks his opponents. Many people also judge him by the number of trophies he wins.

(From the second paragraph: 'a successful leader distinguishes himself by being able to lead by example ...')

answers.label: Q.1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: He believes the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, accepts defeat with dignity and celebrates victory decently, respects others, puts the team's glory above his own and learns from failure.
answers.solution:
A great leader believes that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. He accepts defeat with dignity and celebrates victory decently, and he always respects others. He sacrifices personal glory for the team's success, and he does not despise failure but treats it as his teacher.

(From the second half of the second paragraph.)

answers.label: Q.1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: A successful leader has the qualities of a good captain and wins; a great leader also puts the team above himself, stays dignified in victory and defeat, and learns from failure.
answers.solution:
A successful leader has the qualities of a good captain and wins matches, often because his team is strong. A great leader has something more: he believes the team is greater than any one player, sacrifices his personal glory for the team, stays dignified in both victory and defeat, and learns from his failures.

(The author says it is unfair to put the two together, 'for the former lacks something the latter has'.)

answers.label: Q.1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Popular (looks, humour, cheerfulness); famous (milestones, leading from the front); remembered (trophies); controversial (aggressive, audacious); notorious (above the game); respected (respect for rules); marked out (thinking on their feet).
answers.solution:
The author classifies captains by what they are known for. Some are popular for their looks, wit, humour or cheerful nature. Some are famous for personal milestones and leading from the front, and some are remembered for the trophies they won. Some are controversial for being aggressive and audacious, some are notorious for thinking they are bigger than the game, some are respected for honouring the rules, and some stand out because they can think on their feet.

(From the first paragraph.)

answers.label: Q.1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Leading by example; communicating well; taking the right decisions; staying calm in a crisis; learning from failure.
answers.solution:
As a leader, I would love to lead by example and communicate well with my team. I would like to take the right decisions, remain calm in times of crisis and treat failure as a teacher, so that I keep improving and help my team give its best.

(Any five good qualities from the passage are acceptable; this is a personal answer.)

answers.label: Q.1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) a sacred cow; (ii) think on their feet
answers.solution:
(i) a custom or belief which is highly respected: **a sacred cow** ('treating the rules of the game as a sacred cow')
(ii) react to something effectively without prior thought: **think on their feet** ('being able to think on their feet')

answers.label: Q.1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) despise; (ii) calm; (iii) aggressive
answers.solution:
(i) respect: **despise** ('he does not despise failure')
(ii) nervous: **calm** ('remain calm in times of crises')
(iii) submissive: **aggressive** ('pugnacious, aggressive and audacious'; 'pugnacious' or 'audacious' would also be accepted)

answers.label: Q.2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: The phone can do countless clever things, while the poet cannot even work out how to make a simple call on it.
answers.solution: The phone can do countless clever things, like showing TV, weather and the internet and checking his blood pressure, while the poet cannot even work out how to make a simple phone call on it. So he feels the phone is smart and he is not.

answers.label: Q.2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: It can check his blood pressure and temperature without any examination of his body.
answers.solution: The poet is amazed that the phone can check his blood pressure and temperature 'without even probing all my apertures', that is, without any examination of his body. He had never imagined a phone could do this.

answers.label: Q.2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Discovering that the phone has a camera, so he can take photos and selfies.
answers.solution: The poet's 'Eureka moment' comes when he discovers the phone has a camera: 'A camera..... a CAMERA! Now I can take shots'. He is excited that he can now click photos of everyone and even take a 'selfie'.

answers.label: Q.2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: Mr. Bell invented the telephone; even he would be amazed at what today's phone can do.
answers.solution: Mr. Bell (Alexander Graham Bell) invented the telephone. The poet mentions him to show how far the phone has come: the things a smartphone does today would amaze even the man who invented the telephone.

answers.label: Q.2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: Despite all its gadgets, he does not know how to make a simple phone call on it.
answers.solution: The poet worries that, with all its gadgets and features, he still does not know how to do the simplest thing: make a phone call. (He also notes how costly the phone is.)

answers.label: Q.2(f)
answers.finalAnswer: (i) gizmos; (ii) probing
answers.solution:
(i) gadgets: **gizmos** ('Despite all the gizmos that strike me with awe')
(ii) to examine: **probing** ('Without even probing all my apertures')

answers.label: Q.2(g)
answers.finalAnswer: Metaphor
answers.solution: The figure of speech is a **metaphor**. The poet's unanswered question is spoken of as if it were food stuck in his throat ('craw'), showing that it keeps troubling him.

answers.label: Q.2(h)
answers.finalAnswer: Smart Phone, Not-So-Smart Me
answers.solution: A suitable title: **Smart Phone, Not-So-Smart Me** (or 'My Smart Phone'). It sums up the poem: the phone is clever, but the poet cannot even make a call with it.

answers.label: Q.2(i)
answers.finalAnswer: Greece / geese; Bell / tell
answers.solution: Two pairs of rhyming words: **Greece / geese** and **Bell / tell**. (Other pairs: not / got, too / do, shoot / hoot, craw / awe, all / call.)

answers.label: Q.4
answers.finalAnswer: Article: online learning is the future of education, with its advantages and the need to balance it with classrooms.
answers.solution:
**Online Learning is the Future of Education**
by Arjun, Class VII

The lockdown of 2020 closed our schools, but learning did not stop. Classes moved to mobile phones and laptops, and online learning became part of every student's life.

Online learning has many advantages. A student can learn from the best teachers in the country while sitting at home. Lessons can be recorded and watched again. Videos, animations and quizzes make difficult topics easy to understand, and it saves time and money spent on travel.

However, it also has problems. Many children do not have a phone or a good internet connection, and long hours on a screen harm the eyes.

If these problems are solved, online learning, mixed with classroom teaching, will surely be the future of education.

answers.label: Q.6
answers.finalAnswer: Letter to the editor on the harm cheap notes and guides do to students.
answers.solution:
12, Rajpur Road
Dehradun
10 December 2020

The Editor
The Times of India
New Delhi

Subject: Harm caused by cheap notes and guides

Sir,

Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the harm that cheap notes and guides are doing to students.

These books give ready-made answers to every question. Students stop reading their textbooks and stop thinking for themselves. They learn answers by heart without understanding them, so their creativity and language skills suffer. Many guides are full of mistakes, which students copy into their answer sheets. They also waste the money of poor parents.

Teachers and parents should encourage children to study from textbooks, and the government should check the sale of such books.

Yours faithfully,
Ankit Verma

answers.label: Q.7
answers.finalAnswer: Story with title about a white horse galloping, based on the picture.
answers.solution:
**The Brave White Horse**

Raja was a beautiful white horse who lived on a farm near a forest. He loved to gallop across the fields, his mane flying in the wind.

One dark night, the farmer's little son, Mohan, fell ill with a high fever. The telephone was not working and the doctor lived in a village ten kilometres away. The farmer was worried. Mohan's elder sister quickly climbed onto Raja's back and rode into the night.

Raja galloped faster than ever before. He crossed the stream and the forest without stopping. Within an hour they reached the doctor's house and brought him back to the farm. The doctor treated Mohan, and by morning the boy was smiling again.

From that day, everyone in the village called Raja 'the brave white horse'.

answers.label: Q.8
answers.finalAnswer: (a) He is arrogant, but he is very helpful.; (b) No sooner did he reach the station than he saw his cousin.; (c) What a beautiful house you have!; (d) It is very difficult for me to tell you where he lives.; (e) We want to know the reason for his absence yesterday.; (f) Who would not love to see Dhoni play for India for a few more years?; (g) He said to me, "Did you see the girl yesterday?"; (h) Were you told by somebody to write the assignment again?; (i) In spite of being wise, he is lazy.; (j) Did someone name them Trendsetters yesterday?
answers.solution:
(a) He is arrogant, but he is very helpful. (Two main clauses joined by 'but'.)
(b) No sooner did he reach the station than he saw his cousin.
(c) What a beautiful house you have!
(d) It is very difficult for me to tell you where he lives. (The noun clause 'where he lives' makes it complex.)
(e) We want to know the reason for his absence yesterday. (The clause 'why he was absent' becomes the phrase 'the reason for his absence'.)
(f) Who would not love to see Dhoni play for India for a few more years?
(g) He said to me, "Did you see the girl yesterday?" ('the previous day' becomes 'yesterday'.)
(h) Were you told by somebody to write the assignment again?
(i) In spite of being wise, he is lazy. (One finite verb only.)
(j) Did someone name them Trendsetters yesterday? (The doer is not given, so 'someone' is used.)

answers.label: Q.14
answers.finalAnswer: were; is; was; is; is; has; was; is; has; was
answers.solution:
1. He and I **were** playing. (Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.)
2. English as well as Urdu **is** taught here. (The verb agrees with the first subject.)
3. Neither of the two men **was** very strong. ('Neither' is singular.)
4. Ten kilometres **is** a long walk. (A distance taken as one amount is singular.)
5. No news **is** good news. ('News' is singular.)
6. Many a man **has** done so. ('Many a' takes a singular verb.)
7. The quality of the mangoes **was** not good. (The subject is 'quality'.)
8. Two-third of the city **is** in ruins. (A fraction of a singular noun takes a singular verb.)
9. The United States **has** a big navy. (The name of one country is singular.)
10. The ship with its members **was** lost. (The subject is 'the ship'; 'with its members' does not change it.)

Note: as printed, the parts are labelled (a), (b), (a), (b), (c) ... (h), and 'Two-third' should read 'Two-thirds'.
